name: George Washington
role: Commander of the Continental Army, first President of the United States (1789-1797)
summary: A Virginia planter and general who presided over the Constitutional Convention and, as president, built a strong, well-financed national government under the Constitution. He warned against party spirit, permanent foreign alliances and the weakening of the Union, held that religion and morality support republican government, and backed liberty of conscience for all. He enslaved people throughout his life, and his will freed those he owned after his wife's death.

public-ownership.rationale: Inferred: he stated that, as a general rule, manufactures on public account are inexpedient, with an exception for military supplies.

property-fundamental.rationale: Describes government's task as maintaining all in the secure and tranquil enjoyment of the rights of person and property; his own landholdings were large.

strong-leader.rationale: Warned that the spirit of party leads people to seek security in one man's absolute power, and that consolidating powers in one hand creates despotism; also left office after two terms.

state-harmful.rationale: Calls a government of vigor, with powers properly distributed, indispensable and the surest guardian of liberty; says liberty is little else than a name where government is too feeble to protect person and property.

limit-guns.rationale: Said a free people ought not only to be armed but disciplined, and wanted a uniform militia plan, so favoured an armed citizenry rather than strict limits.

decide-locally.rationale: Held that a government for the whole is indispensable and that vigor in the general government protects liberty, with subdivisions as auxiliary agency.

more-religion-public.rationale: Declared religion and morality indispensable supports, proclaimed days of national thanksgiving and prayer, and opened his presidency with a public prayer, while backing liberty of conscience for all.

gradual-change.rationale: Urges resisting the spirit of innovation upon the Constitution's principles and says time, habit and experience, not mere hypothesis, must test changes to government.

nation-first.rationale: Said it is folly to look for disinterested favors from another nation and that real favors between nations are an illusion, while insisting on good faith and justice toward all.

revolution-justified.rationale: Commanded the Continental Army in a revolution against the Crown; the Farewell Address also affirms the people's right to establish and alter government, though by peaceful constitutional means.

central-planning.rationale: Inferred: he stated that, as a general rule, manufactures on public account are inexpedient.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Signed the 1789 tariff, enacted partly to protect developing manufactures, and asked Congress to encourage manufactures and promote those that make the country independent for military supplies.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Called manufactures on public account generally inexpedient but recommended state-run production of military supplies as an exception, and favored public aid to agriculture boards; mixed.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Signed the 1791 act chartering the Bank of the United States as part of Hamilton's financial program.

one-party-rule.rationale: Warns solemnly against the spirit of party, and says alternate domination of factions ends in despotism; governments by election should not encourage it.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Inferred: he described the republican form of government as the object of his service and the American experiment, and spoke of monarchical governments as a different sort from popular ones.

right-to-secede.rationale: Treats the indissoluble union under one federal head as essential, calls the Union a main prop of liberty, and says to distrust those who try to weaken its bands.

political-violence-never.rationale: Led the Revolutionary War as commander, and as president called out the militia to put down the Whiskey insurrection by force.

separate-church-state.rationale: Gave government no role in compelling belief (to bigotry no sanction) yet issued prayer proclamations at Congress's request; so not strictly separated.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Treated defense, enforcement of laws and courts as public functions: asked for a national army, navy and militia plan, and relied on courts and federal marshals.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Asked citizens to sacrifice individual advantages to the interest of the community and called obedience to law a duty of every individual.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Said experience is the surest standard for testing a constitution and that changes based on mere hypothesis and opinion expose a country to perpetual change.

direct-action.rationale: Condemns obstructions to the laws and combinations that would counteract constituted authorities, and says change must come by an explicit act of the whole people in constitutional forms; led the 1794 response to the western Pennsylvania resistance.

taxation-theft.rationale: Says there can be no payment of debts without revenue and no revenue without taxes, and as president backed the 1790 excise and put down armed resistance to it.

total-state.rationale: Presented liberty as the basis of the government and called for a government of vigor consistent with security of liberty; proposed public encouragement of science and agriculture, not direction of all life.

universal-morality.rationale: Speaks of the immutable principles of private morality and the eternal rules of order and right which Heaven itself has ordained, binding every nation.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Urges discharging debts in peacetime and avoiding the accumulation of debt, not throwing the burden on posterity, and using credit sparingly.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Writes that reason and experience forbid expecting national morality to prevail without religious principle, and calls religion and morality indispensable supports of political prosperity.

national-mission.rationale: Hoped the country would be an example of exalted justice to mankind but urged non-entanglement, not spreading its government abroad.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Asked Congress for a national university, a military academy, post roads, boards to promote agriculture with public money, a navy and encouragement of manufactures, so he did not limit government to defence, justice and property.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Inferred: he wrote that all citizens possess alike liberty of conscience and government assists no persecution.

consent-of-governed.rationale: States that the basis of American political systems is the right of the people to make and alter their constitutions, and calls the government the offspring of the nation's own choice.

separated-powers.rationale: Stresses the necessity of reciprocal checks by dividing and distributing power among different depositaries, and warns that encroachment of one department on another leads to despotism.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Argued that officers' pay needs revising because low pay would exclude talent and virtue unaccompanied by wealth, which he called repugnant to the vital principles of government.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Inferred: he warned that a nation that accepts favors from others pays with a portion of its independence, and he sought to keep the nation free of foreign political ties.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Declined a third term and wrote his Farewell Address to retire, though the Constitution did not bar a third term; he did not argue for a legal limit.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Urged steering clear of permanent alliances and temporary alliances only in emergencies, but said existing engagements must be observed in good faith, so he did not call for ending them.

people-in-arms.rationale: Wanted a disciplined militia but also asked for a regular army, a navy and a military academy, and vetoed a bill discharging dragoons in favor of regular troops.

collective-defense.rationale: Warned against entangling the country in European quarrels through permanent alliances, saying temporary alliances for extraordinary emergencies suffice.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Wished his office to be free of party animosities and local prejudices, and warned against party spirit in elective governments; remained impartial between Jefferson and Hamilton in cabinet.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Inferred: he held that authority rests on the voluntary consent of the people and took the title Mr. President, not a sacred title.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Says the Constitution is sacredly obligatory on all till the people change it, and at his own inauguration he accepted constitutional punishment and public censure if he knowingly violated it.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Inferred: he wrote that all citizens have liberty of conscience and that government gives no assistance to persecution.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: In 1789 invited Congress to weigh amendments, expressing regard for the characteristic rights of freemen and asking how far they could be impregnably fortified; the Bill of Rights passed in his first term.

elective-rulers.rationale: Presents governments purely elective as the popular form he supported, and the republican model as the experiment entrusted to Americans.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Sent Congress estimates of appropriations needed for the coming year and asked it to provide funds, accepting the legislature's power over spending.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Writes that respect for authority and compliance with laws are duties enjoined by liberty, and that the right to establish government presupposes the duty of every individual to obey it.

religion-illusion.rationale: Treats religion as a real support for oaths, morality and popular government, and publicly led thanksgiving and prayer, rather than as an illusion that will fade.

treaties-binding.rationale: Issued proclamations requiring officers and citizens to respect treaties with the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw and others and enforce the trade-and-intercourse law.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Said parties may serve as checks within limits and that the spirit should be mitigated by public opinion, though he condemned self-created societies that obstructed the laws.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Wrote that government gives to bigotry no sanction and to persecution no assistance; separately he recommended prayer by all religious denominations.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Says the basis of government is the right of the people to make and alter constitutions, while acknowledging Providence's role in the founding.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Says to be prepared for war is one of the most effectual means of preserving peace, and sought a regular army, navy and military academy.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Proclaimed neutrality in 1793 and in the Farewell Address urged steering clear of permanent alliances and entanglement in European rivalries.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Prayed for a government of wise, just and constitutional laws discreetly and faithfully executed, and spoke of equal laws of a common government.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Called religion and morality indispensable supports of the nation, so would reject state promotion of atheism.

abolish-ip.rationale: Inferred: he asked Congress to give effectual encouragement to useful inventions and to the exertions of skill and genius.

arms-reduction.rationale: Warned against overgrown military establishments as hostile to republican liberty yet wanted a respectable defensive posture.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Told the House that foreign negotiations require caution and often depend on secrecy, and refused to hand over the Jay Treaty instructions.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Wrote that all possess alike liberty of conscience and immunities of citizenship, and addressed a Jewish congregation as equal citizens.

national-church-status.rationale: Inferred: he wrote that all possess alike liberty of conscience and immunities of citizenship, and called on all religious denominations to give thanks.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Proclaimed against settlers and armed bands violating treaty lines and Indian lands (e.g., James O'Fallon's Kentucky force) and ordered legal punishment of invaders of Cherokee towns.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Said the Constitution and laws bind until changed by the whole people and that obstructing laws is destructive of liberty.

notes: On slavery, he was a lifelong slaveholder who wrote in 1786 that he wished to see gradual abolition by legislative authority and would not buy more slaves, and in 1799 freed those he held in his own right (not the dower slaves) at his wife's death. Slavery-specific record, such as the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 and the Naturalization Act of 1790 limited to free white persons, was left null where no statement matches. Several answers rest on one or two passages in Farewell Address and annual messages; the Newburgh Address, Founders Online papers and Jay Treaty text itself were not available to the auditor.
